summary: Teach subtracting multiples of ten (e.g. 70−30) through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens = four tens. The known fact 7−3=4 is reused at the scale of tens, so the '0' in 40 carries real place meaning rather than being appended as a trick. Removable tens-materials, bead strings, and number lines that jump in tens make this visible; contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit.
misconceptions: Dropping the ten-unit: subtracting 7−3=4 and answering 4 instead of 40
Treating the zero as a spelling trick ('add a zero') with no unit meaning
Counting back in ones (70,69,68…) and losing track
Confusing 70−3 with 70−30 because the unit isn't tracked

activities.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
steps: Lay out seven ten-rods (or ten-sticks/strips of ten) to represent 70.
For 70 − 30, physically remove three whole rods and say the running count aloud: 70 → 60 → 50 → 40.
Name what is left as 'four tens, which is 40', pointing at the four rods rather than counting individual cubes.
Say the matching single-digit fact: 'seven tens minus three tens is four tens, just like 7 − 3 = 4.'
Repeat for 80 − 50 (eight rods, remove five, leaving three = 30) and 90 − 60 (nine rods, remove six, leaving three = 30), each time removing whole rods and stating the answer in tens.
activities.insight: Subtracting multiples of ten is the same subtraction as the known single-digit fact, spoken in units of ten; the zero in the answer is a real placeholder showing zero ones, which keeps the 4 in the tens place. It is not decoration.

activities.title: Contrasting 70 − 3 with 70 − 30
steps: Work 70 − 30 by removing three whole ten-rods; record the answer (40) and the running count.
Rebuild 70 with seven ten-rods, then unbundle (or exchange) one ten-rod for ten single cubes; use these to work 70 − 3 by removing three single cubes.
Compare the two results: 70 − 30 = 40 (a big change) versus 70 − 3 = 67 (a small change).
Explain in words why removing three tens changes the number far more than removing three ones.
activities.insight: The size of the unit being removed matters: subtracting tens and subtracting ones are different because each ten is worth ten ones.

activities.title: Linking the known fact on a reference chart
steps: Look at 70 and state that it is '7 tens'.
Do the same for other decade pairs (e.g. 8 − 5 = 3 beside 80 − 50 = 30), reading each as a statement about tens.
activities.insight: Each decade subtraction reuses a single-digit fact at the scale of tens, so the known fact gives the answer directly.

activities.title: Decade subtraction practice with the dropped-unit trap
steps: Complete a short sequence of decade subtractions (e.g. 70−30, 60−40, 90−50), writing each answer.
For 70 − 30, choose the correct answer from options that include 4 as a tempting wrong answer, and explain why 4 is wrong.
activities.insight: Consolidate the tens strategy and catch the common error of dropping the ten-unit.

activities.title: Optional: rhythmic count-back in tens
steps: Chant the tens count-back sequence aloud with a rhythm: '70, 60, 50, 40' for 70 − 30.
Match the number of jumps to the number of tens being removed.
activities.insight: The tens count-sequence becomes fluent and the 'jump in tens' becomes a natural move.

checkQuestion: Set these to work one at a time and watch how the child does them: 70 − 30, 80 − 50, 90 − 60. Then hand them ten-rods and ask them to build 80 − 50 and tell you the answer and how they know.
checkAnswer: 40, 30, 30. Efficient: treat each as tens — seven tens minus three tens is four tens, 40 — or subtract the tens digits keeping the ten-unit (the zero). With rods, remove five ten-rods from eight, leaving three ten-rods = 30.
